chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Safwan and Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has a specified volume of grain owed to me, and he sends me loads containing less than the volume owed to me, so I accept them as a gamble (mujazafah). He said, 'There is no harm in it.'

He said, And I asked him about a man who has a hundred kurrs of dates owed to another man, and the debtor has an unowned/abandoned date palm grove, so he says to the creditor, 'Give me this palm grove of yours in exchange for what is owed to you.' It seemed he disliked this.

He said, And I asked him about two men who share a date palm grove, so one says to the other, 'Choose: either you take this palm grove for such and such a specified volume of grain, and give me half of that volume, whether it increases or decreases; or I take it for that.' He said, 'There is no harm in it.'

key_terms.زَادَ أَوْ نَقَصَ: Whether it increases or decreases (referring to variable yield/quantity).
key_terms.مُجَازَفَةً: Gambling or guessing; a transaction where the exact quantity or value is uncertain at the time of exchange.
key_terms.مُسَمًّى: Specified or designated (referring to a known quantity).
key_terms.نَخْلٌ سَائِبَةٌ: An unowned or abandoned date palm grove.

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to settle a debt with goods of uncertain quantity in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the boundaries of *al-Gharar* (uncertainty) in commercial contracts, distinguishing between permissible estimation and prohibited ambiguity. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) permits accepting variable quantities of debt repayment (such as dates) as a settlement, reflecting the practical flexibility of Shia jurisprudence in trade, while expressing mild disapproval (*karah*) for specific forms of barter that introduce greater uncertainty. This ruling underscores the principle that minor, calculable uncertainty does not invalidate a contract, provided the essential elements are clear.
